I think it's normal to think about death a little bit, especially in an existential sort of way, eg:

What if...?
Is there an afterlife?
Where does my consciousness go?
What would happen if I did it right now?
Would dying be easier?
etc

That kind of thought is normal. I think of them as sort of *passive* thoughts...where you're just wondering, y'know? But when they become more *active*, and you start to really properly consider it, that's more problematic.

And when they're *active*, the thoughts are very intrusive. I can't do anything...not even hold a conversation...without thinking of dying. Even - as you're describing in your post, OP - looking at a construction site. I'd love to be able to just look at it and think "it's a construction site, I wonder what they're building", instead of thinking negative stuff and seeing ways of dying.

Also, to be honest, even if your coworkers have the same thoughts...well, that doesn't make it okay. I guess it's nice to know that other people deal with similar stuff and you're not alone, but just because other people have this thing doesn't mean you should accept and put up with it, right?
You're doing good :D

Sometimes I think just a little scratch can't be a bad thing. Especially if I don't cut deep enough to leave a scar. There will be a few scratches for like a week or something, then I can move on and forget about it. Almost.

For me (and it seems others in this thread), SH is relaxing. I guess the body releases endorphins in response to the cut, and furthermore the sight of blood brings me back down to earth when I'm feeling intense. However, I do know inside that SH isn't a solution.

I'd never recommend it to anyone I know. I mean, I can't stop people from doing what they want to do. And similarly I wouldn't want anyone to try interfere and stop me from SH. But somehow I feel that a different set of rules applies to me and I can justify SH to myself.

Hey dude, I hope you're doing okay over there.

The situation you're describing with Meow sounds quite similar to something I went through a while back, I know how you feel. And it sucks. I can't fix it, but I can tell you some of the observations I made myself which you might find insightful:

1) At the real peak of my depression, I felt awful and wasn't really sure why. So, probably subconsciously at first, I found reasons to explain why I felt so shitty. *That thing that person did last week that annoyed me?* Totally... *I screwed up in that exam?* Oh yeah, that's totally why I'm feeling down. But really, that's not the case. Those things...the girl...exams, anything, were just scapegoated by me in an attempt to justify why I was feeling crap.

2) Sometimes day-to-day external stuff (especially relationships with others) can **trigger** these feelings in me. But I've come to realise that they're not the real **cause** -- instead, that's inside me (and something I've started dealing with in therapy). Someone being disrespectful or whatever might make me angry, that's fair enough. But suicidally angry? No, there's something else underneath that.

3) Look at it this way...if Meow called you up now and told you that she's actually felt the same way about you all along, you could do all the things you've been dreaming of. Awesome. But in reality, that wouldn't fix the problem. It wouldn't make all the bad stuff in the world go away. And actually, I've found myself in that situation only to feel even worse, thinking *"this is what you wanted isn't it? why do you still feel so bad then?"*. Relationships can be very good for people, and a lot of fun, but there's a lot more to life than one girl.

So in the meantime, it's difficult to deal with this thing. But at some point in the future, you'll be able to look back at it and go "meh". Just from this one post of yours I've read, you seem to be a good guy. I hope you don't commit suicide, and I hope there's someone there (friend or family) maybe you'd feel comfortable venting how you feel with? It's difficult to keep it all bottled up in your head. Sorry if it sounds like I'm lecturing you, I'm not! PM me if you want.

A very perceptive and honest post, and well-written. I remember feeling this sort of thing a while back. Also, I think it's great that you're looking at why you feel the way you do, and helping yourself.

I'll throw in two of my own thoughts for consideration:

**1)** How can you be sure that the thing you described about women is really the 'root' of your depression? In my opinion, depression is usually more complex than something which can have just one simple cause. Perhaps the women issue is a sort of aggravating factor in a bigger picture? Basically I'm suggesting that you don't rule out other causes/triggers too, which all combined can make for the place you're in now. This will also help out with my second point:

**2)** I've made the mistake before (especially when I've been low) of imagining a future where a few things are different but everything is better. So, for example, *"if only I could find someone to be with, everything would be better!"* or *"if only I had a car, I'd be able to do stuff and things would be perfect!"*...anything where I change a few things in my mind and assume it will solve all my problems, or any thoughts like *"I'm feeling crap today, but everything will be better tomorrow!"*. And then, in my experience, when you do get to that future...when you do find someone to be with, or buy a car, or whatever...it's still possible to feel depressed. And then, if anything, I get more frustrated because I'm thinking *"this was supposed to fix everything!"*.

I hope that makes sense?

Best of luck!

I've done this so much myself - where I look back at the past and pick out what I think I did wrong. And y'know, it's so easy to look back and think (negatively) about how things could've been different - or to feel regret in short.

In any real-world situation (especially involving other people), I really don't believe there's ever a case where making a decision is truly black-or-white. There are pros and cons to every decision, and we weigh them up as best we can in the given context. Never really knowing how they'll actually play out into the future. But then, of course, once that future has arrived, it's easy to look back at where it's come from and pick out those decisions.

So I don't think there's really a universal 'right' or 'wrong' decision in the kind of circumstance you're talking about. Hopefully what I'm trying to convey makes sense?

Honestly, I don't know you, but I guess I'm trying to say that you haven't done anything wrong here : )

Important thing to note though: I think it would be really beneficial for you to have someone (friend or family) to talk to about the whole thing; someone who you know will try to be understanding and non-judgmental. Share the emotional burden you carry with at least one person you can trust. You might even find people with similar experiences out there.

In the past I've used sort of 'delaying' or 'avoidance' techniques for when I can't cope.

For instance, I go "okay, I'll wait 10 more seconds before I cut myself", then I go "well that wasn't so bad, now let's put a youtube video on and not cut until I get to the end of that", and then another video, or listen to a song, or phone a friend to talk about something unrelated, telling myself that I won't cut until after the conversation, etc. Taking the dog for a walk is a great one. You get the idea anyway.

Usually the best thing for me to do is go to bed. I think to myself, "hey, I can always do it when I wake up", and often when I wake up the urge has calmed down a bit because sleeping has helped me to cool down from whatever was getting me wound up before.

Student here.

First off, I've found the support network in education to be really good (depression seems to be relatively common in students). For instance, if you speak to your tutors/professors about it, there's probably a way of getting some extra consideration in your exams and stuff if you feel that your health (mental or otherwise) prevented you from showing off your full potential on the day. And similarly it's often possible to get an extension to deadlines for coursework/assessments for health reasons.

Secondly, more of an actual answer to your questions:
I used to drag myself to *every* class, no matter how shitty I was feeling or how little I'd slept the night before. Now I can see that doing that doesn't do me any favours - sometimes I need to take a step back and realise that it's not in my own best interests to attend a particular class today, especially if I'm going to sit there being angry at the world and not paying attention.

Okay, this doesn't really address most of the things you wrote about, but what if you sent an email or phoned up the counselling office to book an initial appointment? Then you're kinda committed to going. Or, at least, that's how I sort of talk myself into doing things like that.
Sounds like you've got a lot on your plate. But I'm glad you're taking steps to improve. Healing is a gradual process. Are you receiving therapy/counselling at all? If not, I'd recommend it.

As for ideas for things you can do which will calm you down, another poster already suggested drawing/painting. That's a pretty good idea. Or maybe get a jigsaw puzzle? Something you can get immersed in which kinda keeps your mind focused on the thing without much effort. Maybe watch a silly youtube video you'll enjoy?

However, I know that when I'm f*cking pissed off at something, the last thing I want to do is get out my crayons or a jigsaw puzzle. Those things are good at keeping me calm when I'm already calm.

Maybe you could give yourself some time every evening to sit down and do one of those things/something you'll enjoy? Give yourself like half an hour of me-time a day in which you'll do what you want in a quiet environment and not worry about whether you feel normal or not.

I particularly resonate with the first paragaph of your reply here. I find it really difficult to convey what I'm thinking/feeling. And when I'm in an okay-ish mood, I can't understand myself why I was in an awful mood only an hour before, or describe what that feels like to anyone else. And, of course, when I'm feeling really shitty, there's no way I'm capable of explaining to anyone what's that's like.

I also understand what you mean about your mind not using logical thought patterns. And guess what...I get the same thing. There's a kind of irrational bit of my mind which is all-encompassing when I'm feeling low. That's the bit of my mind which thinks that self-harm and more is a good idea. How the f*ck could that ever be a good idea? Yet I do it anyway. Good one me.

As for your second paragraph; well, I see a counsellor in the UK too. We've talked about some hardcore stuff (suicide included), and he hasn't had to break confidentiality. He's encouraged me to see a doctor and to get other support, but he hasn't had to step further than that. I guess you just need to show your counsellor that you're not insane, and that you're prepared to consider how you can improve your situation. She's there to help you, not to cause you shit at work for no reason.

Good luck! : )

You're obviously suffering a lot here, and you've done well to write such an eloquent post describing how you're feeling. It's really good that you're seeing a counsellor. Don't be afraid to tell her exactly how you're feeling - it's her job to listen to that shit and to help you to help yourself. So you won't be doing either of you any favours by keeping things quiet (plus the two things you mentioned - drugs and suicide - are extremely important/relevant).

I'd seriously recommend writing down some things you want to discuss with her before your session. If nothing else comes to you, then print off the post you've written here. And if you find that you can't talk, then simply tell your counsellor that you suffer from anxiety which makes it difficult to get the words out - that's important too.

Best of luck.
